headline: Let existing columns prescribe the next row prefix
statement: Given unique lowercase words of equal length, return every word square that can be built from them. A square has as many rows as the word length and its row r equals column r. A word may be reused in different rows. Return squares in any order; row order within a square matters.
prerequisites: Basic Python lists, loops, and functions
constraints: All words have the same length from 1 through 4.
Words contain lowercase letters and are unique.
intuition: In a word square, row r and column r must spell the same word. When choosing the next row, its first letters are already fixed by the earlier rows. Use a prefix index to find only words that start with those letters, then try each possible continuation.
approach: Index each word under its proper prefixes, including the empty prefix; full-length prefixes are never queried.
At depth k, build the required prefix by reading square[r][k] for all r<k.
Try every indexed word with that prefix, allowing reuse.
Save a copy when k reaches the word length.
correctness: Each newly appended row matches every existing row at their crossing positions. This invariant guarantees symmetry at completion. Conversely, a valid square always has the prescribed prefix at every depth, so each of its rows is considered. Since input words are unique, each row sequence is produced once.
bruteForce: Try all W^L sequences of L words and check row-column equality afterward. Prefix pruning rejects invalid partial squares immediately.

complexity.time: O(W * L^2 + L * W^L) worst case
complexity.space: O(W * L^2 + L) auxiliary, excluding output
complexity.explanation: W words of length L are indexed under L copied proper prefixes. Worst-case search is exponential in L, which is at most four; output and branch prefix work are bounded by L.

pitfalls: Allow repeated use of the same word; no used set is needed.
Read column k from existing rows to form the prefix.
Do not sort rows inside a returned square.
